# Decisions

**GENERATED by tools/generate_decisions.py — do not edit.**
Regenerate with `make docs`; `tests/test_decisions.py` fails if the committed
file and the generator disagree.

B6. Questions this review reached and deliberately did not answer, because the
answer is a product call rather than an engineering one.

## Why this is generated

The roadmap said there were **nine**, "listed at the end of" the review log.
Auditing that found three things wrong at once: there were five, they were
recorded in two different notations, two of them sat mid-document rather than at
the end — and **one had already been answered.** DEC-10 asked for real token
revocation; B5 built it; the document went on asking for a pass.

That last one is why this file is generated rather than written. **Each decision
declares what would resolve it, as a check against the code**, and the state
below is derived. A decision cannot go on asking a question the code has settled,
and cannot be marked settled before it is.

It is the only part of this a machine can own. What each option costs, and which
to take, is written out and left to a person — with a recommendation, because
three options and no opinion is a way of not helping.

## The state `decided`, and why it had to be added

The first version of this file derived two states from the check: it passes, or
it does not. Then these questions started getting answered, and answering one is
not the same as building it — a decision can live in a sibling checkout, or be a
choice to change nothing, or deliberately leave code in the tree. Each of those
rendered as `open`.

Which is the same failure the file was written to fix, one level up. `open` sends
a reader to ask for a decision; a reader who acts on it goes and asks for one
that has already been made. So there is a fourth state, and it outranks
`unknown` on purpose: a person choosing is a fact about the world, not about this
repository, and a check that cannot reach a sibling checkout does not make the
choice unknown.

A `decided` entry carries a **Decided** paragraph saying what was chosen. The
recommendation above it is left as it was written, including where it declined
to recommend — what engineering thought before the call is worth more than a
register that reads as though it had always agreed.

| State | Count | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `open` | 0 | Nobody has decided |
| `decided` | 3 | A person chose; the code does not show it yet |
| `answered` | 3 | The check says the code has settled it |
| `unknown` | 0 | The check could not look, or cannot tell |

| | Question | State | Touches |
|---|---|---|---|
| DEC-10 | Should a signed token be revocable while the account exists? | `answered` | `AC-11` |
| DEC-11 | Where does a customer get their updates? | `decided` | `DP-5` |
| DEC-12 | Should the retired landing page stay routed? | `answered` | — |
| DEC-13 | The Celery worker and Flower serve a queue nothing writes to. Wire it or remove it? | `answered` | — |
| DEC-14 | Should the CLI keep defaulting `api_url` to a vendor host? | `decided` | `DP-5` |
| DEC-15 | Is thirty days the right token lifetime, now that revocation exists? | `decided` | — |

## DEC-10 — Should a signed token be revocable while the account exists?

**`answered`.** Raised in §89, F122.

**What waiting costs.** None any more. This is the entry that made the register worth generating: B5 built it and the document went on asking the question for a pass.

**Options.**

* **A deny list in Redis** — Closes it completely, adds a round trip to every request and a new failure mode when Redis is away.
* **Short-lived access tokens with refresh** — The standard answer, and a change to every client including the CLI's stored credential.
* **A `tokens_valid_after` column** — One column, one comparison, on a row the request already reads.

**Recommendation.** The third, and it was built — §89. `POST /v1/portal/me/revoke-sessions` and an org-scoped admin twin, compared against the token's `iat` at F122's single choke point.

## DEC-11 — Where does a customer get their updates?

**`decided`.** Raised in F126.

**What waiting costs.** A self-hosted install contacts `github.com/ignite-ember/igni/releases` on launch unless the customer turns checking off. It is the one outbound host a default install has, which sits awkwardly beside DP-5 — and an air-gapped customer cannot update at all.

**Options.**

* **A configurable endpoint** — Tauri 2 supports it. The customer mirrors releases and points the app at their own host; signature verification is unchanged because the pubkey is separate from the address, so a mirror cannot substitute a build.
* **Updates through the customer's own igni server** — Tidier for the operator, and it makes the server a release distribution point it currently is not.
* **Leave it and document it** — One outbound host, off by one setting.

**Recommendation.** The first. It changes what a release *is* — a mirrored artefact somebody publishes — which is why it is a decision rather than a change.

**Decided.** A configurable endpoint. It lives in `igni`, so this reads `decided` until the Tauri config stops naming a single host — the state that did not exist before this decision was taken.

**On checking this one.** The evidence is in `igni`, a separate repository. Run `make docs-check-siblings` beside a checkout of it to see what the code says today.

## DEC-12 — Should the retired landing page stay routed?

**`answered`.** Raised in §75.

**What waiting costs.** Two landing pages that disagree about the product, one reachable by anyone who guesses the URL: `/old` offers a "Public Beta" badge, a "Download Windows" button to a macOS visitor and a "Pricing" nav item, against a live page that says igni itself is free.

**Options.**

* **Delete it** — What "drop all the backward compat" points at. Nothing links to `/old` from anywhere in the app.
* **Keep it deliberately** — As a comparison during design work — and fix its copy so the two pages stop contradicting each other.
* **Keep the route, drop the page** — Redirect `/old` to `/`, the way `/alt` already does, so an old shared link still lands somewhere correct.

**Recommendation.** The third, then the first once nobody is opening it. A public surface disappearing is not a side effect of a baselining task.

**Decided.** Redirect now, delete later. `/old` sends a visitor to `/`, so the contradiction was gone without a public URL vanishing in the same change. The "later" half is done: the page file was deleted on 2026-10-31, before this repository was published, and the redirect stays.

## DEC-13 — The Celery worker and Flower serve a queue nothing writes to. Wire it or remove it?

**`answered`.** Raised in F55, §91.

**What waiting costs.** Production runs a worker at `--concurrency=200`, a Flower container, a Redis database and a Postgres result backend for a queue that is always empty. Re-checked in B8: still no dispatcher, no schedule, and the two services still in the compose file. Meanwhile the docstring's promise — "on a schedule to recover from missed webhooks" — is a real need that nothing meets.

**Options.**

* **Wire the triggers** — An admin endpoint and a schedule. Recovering from missed webhooks is a genuine gap, and the task itself is sound — bounded retries, idempotent upsert, safe to requeue.
* **Remove the worker and Flower** — The pipeline moved to code-index with the rest of the indexing work. Two containers, a Redis database and a result backend come out of the compose file.

**Recommendation.** No recommendation, and that is the point: the two answers are opposite and both plausible. Deleting a worker on the assumption that a feature was abandoned is not a call to make from the outside.

**Decided.** Remove the worker and Flower. Two containers, a Redis database, a Postgres result backend, `celery` and `flower` as dependencies, and a guide to operating all of it came out; the indexing work it was written for lives in `igni__code-index`.

It does not close the gap. Recovering from missed webhooks is still a real need that nothing meets — the same as before, except that the code no longer implies otherwise. It is CodeIndex's to meet: igni server no longer receives webhooks, and repository integration is CodeIndex's (`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`). `tests/test_the_worker_is_gone.py` keeps the removal complete and keeps that sentence from being quietly dropped along with the worker.

## DEC-14 — Should the CLI keep defaulting `api_url` to a vendor host?

**`decided`.** Raised in F94.

**What waiting costs.** DP-5a. The decision is already made — "there is to be no vendor endpoint" — and the change is not: flipping the default to empty would produce malformed requests instead of a clear refusal, so doing it properly means a refusal path at the call sites. It is allow-listed as an open question in the code itself rather than passing quietly.

**Options.**

* **Empty default plus a refusal path** — The F69 pattern: a misconfiguration fails loudly instead of doing something silently wrong. Affects every installed CLI.
* **Keep the default until the cloud routing exists** — The stated future plan is a URL pointing at the customer's own cloud, at which point there is no vendor to default to.

**Recommendation.** The first, and it lives in `igni` — which is why B3 is `blocked` here rather than open.

**Decided.** Empty default plus a refusal path, in `igni`.

**On checking this one.** The evidence is in `igni`, a separate repository. Run `make docs-check-siblings` beside a checkout of it to see what the code says today.

## DEC-15 — Is thirty days the right token lifetime, now that revocation exists?

**`decided`.** Raised in §89.

**What waiting costs.** DEC-10 paired the two questions and answered one. Thirty days was the *only* bound on a leaked credential before B5; it is now the second line behind withdrawal, which is a different trade-off — and nobody has revisited the number since it stopped being the only defence.

**Options.**

* **Leave it at thirty days** — Revocation is the control now, and a shorter window costs every developer a re-authentication they did not need.
* **Shorten it** — A smaller window for a token nobody notices has leaked. The cost is sign-in friction, which for a CLI stored credential is felt.
* **Make it configurable** — The customer decides. Adds a setting to get wrong, and the startup checks would have to bound it.

**Recommendation.** Leave it, and record that it was reconsidered rather than merely inherited. The argument for thirty days is stronger *with* revocation than it was without.

**Decided.** Thirty days, deliberately. The argument is stronger with revocation than it was without: withdrawal is the control now, and a shorter window buys a smaller leak exposure at the cost of a re-authentication every developer would feel. This entry is the record that it was reconsidered rather than inherited — which is the whole of what was missing, and why `decided` is the right state for it rather than `answered`.

**On checking this one.** A decision to keep thirty days deliberately looks identical in the code to never having asked. This is the one entry whose `answered` state a check cannot establish, and saying so is better than a resolver that lies.

## What is not here

**Decisions that are the customer's.** Where inference runs, whether the audit
trail amounts to employee monitoring, what the retention windows should be: the
DPIA and the Article 30 record ask those of a controller, and they are not the
vendor's to make.

**Signatures.** Every `Process` row in the register needs a person, and section C
of the road drafted seven documents to the point of one. That is a different
kind of waiting from a decision: the content exists and nobody has adopted it.

**Anything an engineer can settle.** If a question has a right answer that
evidence establishes, it belongs in the review as a finding rather than here as a
choice. Five of the six entries above were re-checked while writing this file and
one of them turned out to have been settled by code — which is the failure mode a
list of open questions has, and the reason this one is checked.
